sources.excerpt: Large Language Model (LLM) Agents are advancing quickly, with the increasing leveraging of LLM Agents to assist in development tasks such as code generation. While LLM Agents accelerate code generation, studies indicate they may introduce adverse effects on development. However, existing metrics solely measure pass rates, failing to reflect impacts on long-term maintainability and readability, and failing to capture human intuitive evaluations of PR. Evaluation results indicate that LLM Agents frequently disregard code reuse opportunities, resulting in higher levels of redundancy compared to human developers. sources.title: Insights into Security-Related AI-Generated Pull Requests
sources.excerpt: Recent years have experienced growing contributions of AI coding agents that assist human developers in various software engineering tasks. However, this growing AI-assisted autonomy raises questions about security and trust. In this paper, we analyze more than 33,000 AI-generated pull requests (PRs) and identify 675 security-related submissions made by agentic AIs. Then we examine the security-related PRs with a focus on recurring security weaknesses, review outcomes and latency, commit message quality, and rejection reasons. The results show that security-related AI PRs introduce a small set of recurring weaknesses such as regex inefficiencies, injection flaws, and path traversal. Many flawed contributions are still merged, while rejections often arise from social or process factors such as inactivity or missing test coverage. The commit message quality of AI PRs has a limited effect on acceptance or latency, in contrast to human PRs reported in previous studies. We also extend existing rejection taxonomies by adding categories that are unique to AI-generated security contributions. These findings offer new insights into the strengths and shortcomings of autonomous coding systems…

sources.title: These Aren't the Reviews You're Looking For How Humans Review AI-Generated Pull Requests
sources.excerpt: We analyze code review interactions for AI-generated pull requests (PRs) on GitHub using the AIDev dataset and compare them to human-authored PRs within the same repositories. We find that most AI-generated PRs receive no review and, when reviewed, are largely dominated by AI agents rather than humans. Human-authored PRs are more likely to receive human-only review and to attract direct human feedback. In contrast, reviews of AI-generated PRs more often take the form of automation-mediated interaction, with human involvement frequently expressed through agent steering rather than standalone evaluation. These results indicate systematic differences in how review activity is structured in agentic workflows and raise challenges for interpreting review metrics as indicators of human oversight in large-scale mining studies.

sources.title: Augmentation with Dilution: A Large-Scale Empirical Study of Human Contributor Ecosystems After AI Coding Agent Adoption
sources.excerpt: AI coding agents are penetrating open-source software development at an unprecedented pace, yet existing research predominantly treats human contributors as a static backdrop rather than as the subject of inquiry. This paper presents the first large-scale empirical study that takes the human contributor ecosystem as its dependent variable, examining how the number, composition, and behavior of human participants change following AI coding agent adoption in open-source projects. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design on a dataset of 11,097 GitHub repositories spanning January 2023 to May 2026, we provide causal evidence via the Sun and Abraham estimator. Our results show that AI agent adoption does not significantly change the absolute number of human contributors (ATT = 0.014, p = 0.224), but significantly reduces human contributor density (ATT = -0.019, p = 0.002), indicating that the relative share of human participation declines as AI-generated pull requests accumulate. sources.title: "We Permit the Use of AI, but [...]": The Landscape of AI Policies in Popular Open Source Projects
sources.excerpt: Open source communities are converging on a new governance artifact: the AI contribution policy. These policies barely existed a few months ago and are now being written and adopted. We analyzed 281 AI contribution policies, and manually classified them along the six dimensions; to study how policies change, we also tracked 92 dedicated AI policy files over time. We answer four research questions on (1) AI usage allowance, (2) AI disclosure practices, (3) AI slop countermeasures, and (4) AI policy evolution. We find that, first, permission is the norm rather than the exception: 83.3% of policies permit or encourage AI in code contributions. But permission comes with conditions, as 67.3% require a high level of human involvement and 43.4% assign accountability. Second, AI disclosure is required by 48.8% of policies, most often in pull request descriptions and commit messages, but what must be disclosed varies widely. Third, we identify ten countermeasures against AI slop, targeting pull requests, users, and autonomous agents. sources.title: You can contribute if you... An Empirical Framework of AI Contribution Policies in OSS
sources.excerpt: Artificial intelligence is reshaping open source software (OSS) contribution by lowering the cost of producing code, documentation, issue reports, and review interactions. This creates opportunities for broader participation, but also disrupts how maintainers assess contributor effort, competence, and accountability. In response, OSS projects are beginning to regulate AI-mediated contribution through contribution guidelines and other project documentation. This paper presents an empirical study of these emerging policies. We analyze project policies on AI-mediated contributions by evaluating their underlying rationales, rules, and expectations. Based on these findings, we introduce the AI Contribution Governance Framework, which organizes recurring concerns and governance mechanisms across projects. sources.title: An Exploratory Study of Dependabot Cooldown Adoption in Open-Source GitHub Projects
sources.excerpt: Automated dependency updates can rapidly propagate malicious package releases before maintainers and the broader community have enough time to detect them. In July 2025, GitHub made Dependabot cooldown generally available as a defense against software supply chain attacks. However, the effects of its early adoption remain unknown. In this exploratory study, we empirically examine how popular open-source GitHub repositories adopt and configure the feature and investigate their motivations. We find that security concerns motivated 83 of 92 adoption events with known motivations. Security linter warnings triggered 43 of 75 security-only adoptions. Among 251 ecosystems within repositories that retained cooldown, 97.2% set a general delay. Of these, 64.3% used seven days, while use of each update type setting was below 10%. Early adopters therefore favor simple default delays over fine-grained controls. These findings suggest that tools could provide robust defaults reflecting ecosystem support and reserve fine-grained controls for dependencies with clear update priorities.

sources.title: Retire these labels: "good first issue", Package-novice, Package-intermediate, Hacktoberfest
sources.excerpt: Some core maintainers (myself included) feel like the following labels have outlived their usefulness. They were originally created in hope we can use these to recruit and retain future maintainers. However, the cost of triaging mostly unacceptable pull requests (nowadays usually AI slops) have outweighed any benefit. These labels are: - `good first issue` - `Package-novice` - `Package-intermediate` (I don't find intermediate very meaningful, you either need expertise or you don't) - `Hacktoberfest` (we have not participated in many years) - `hacktoberfest-accepted` (same reasoning as `Hacktoberfest`) Proposed actions: - Remove them from open issues/PRs. - Retire them in labels list by prepending with a 💤 (as we do with other labels that went through similar fate) - Remove their mentions from https://www.astropy.org/contribute.html (anywhere else?) Out of scope: - I think the keeping `Package-expert` label is fine, as we still need to identify which issues need serious domain expertise, even amongst ourselves.

problems.title: Low-effort AI-generated pull requests drain maintainer review capacity
problems.statement: Popular open-source projects report a sharp increase in AI-generated pull requests and issues submitted without understanding or follow-up. Reviewing and triaging them consumes scarce maintainer time, and some projects now restrict or close outside contributions entirely.
problems.affectedUsers: Maintainers and moderators of popular open-source projects (evidenced: tldraw, Rust, Astropy, LLVM, Linux, Ghostty, scikit-learn, Zulip, Godot)
problems.severityNote: High. tldraw auto-closes all external PRs, Rust maintainers call it a DDoS on capacity, and several projects threaten bans.
problems.frequencyNote: Recurring across at least 9 projects' policies and issues (Nov 2025 – 2026). A study counted 281 AI contribution policies in popular projects. No direct measurement of inbound volume was retrieved.

problems.title: Compromised maintainer credentials ship malware in popular packages
problems.statement: Attackers who gain a maintainer's registry account, publish token or branch write access publish malicious versions of widely used packages. The 2026 cases include a remote access trojan via axios and a credential stealer via litellm. The maintainers are victims, not insiders.
problems.affectedUsers: Maintainers of popular packages and every downstream consumer
problems.severityNote: Critical: RATs and credential stealers in packages with very large reach.
problems.frequencyNote: At least four distinct incidents in the 2026 signals (axios, litellm, asyncapi, TanStack).

problems.title: Fabricated AI-generated security reports waste triage capacity
problems.statement: Security teams receive confident but fabricated vulnerability reports generated with AI tools. Each one must be investigated with priority, which pulls maintainers away from real work. curl no longer runs a bug bounty because of the incentive for made-up reports.
problems.affectedUsers: Security teams of widely used open-source projects
problems.severityNote: High for affected projects (curl removed its bounty), but evidenced by one origin only in this run.
problems.frequencyNote: Unknown. Secondary reporting could not be retrieved in this session.

problems.title: Minor and patch releases break dependents' code
problems.statement: Package managers install minor and patch updates automatically on the promise that they're backward compatible. When a library breaks that promise, downstream projects break without warning. Users report pinned versions, broken release pipelines and lost weekends.
problems.affectedUsers: Developers and teams depending on npm packages, and maintainers of libraries built on other libraries
problems.severityNote: High when it happens: broken builds and pipelines, and emergency pinning.
problems.frequencyNote: Hundreds of GitHub issues are titled about it. True frequency not yet measured.

problems.title: New releases are installed before malicious ones are detected
problems.statement: Automated and manual installs pick up new versions immediately. Malicious releases are typically detected and removed within hours, but not before they've been installed. Users ask package managers for release-age delays.
problems.affectedUsers: Application and CI pipelines consuming open-source packages
problems.frequencyNote: Popular feature requests on bun (693 reactions) and npm (241).

problems.title: Submission effort no longer signals contributor trustworthiness
problems.statement: Open source used to treat the effort of submitting a change as a signal of a potential long-term contributor. AI tools make plausible-looking submissions nearly free, so maintainers lose that cheap filter and are moving to explicit trust mechanisms that risk excluding newcomers.
problems.affectedUsers: Maintainers, and genuine first-time contributors who face new barriers
problems.frequencyNote: Articulated by LLVM, Vouch/Ghostty, tldraw and Astropy.

problems.title: Trusted publishing can't be bootstrapped on npm
problems.statement: npm's OIDC trusted publishing can't be used for a package's first version, so maintainers must still create a token or publish manually. That keeps long-lived credentials around.
problems.severityNote: Medium: a narrow gap, but it keeps tokens in circulation.

problems.title: Existing semver checkers only see the type surface
problems.statement: The available and emerging checkers compare TypeScript type declarations. Many real breaking releases come from behaviour changes or from package metadata (e.g. a raised Node engine requirement), which those tools don't inspect.
problems.affectedUsers: Maintainers relying on automated checks, and especially packages without TypeScript types
problems.severityNote: Medium: a gap in tooling, not a direct harm.
problems.frequencyNote: All four real complaints examined were non-type breaks (small sample).

competitors.name: AI-authorship PR detectors (pr-slop-filter, deslop-kitten, TuringMerge, …)
competitors.description: GitHub Actions that try to detect AI-generated PRs from textual and diff 'tells' and block or label them. A GitHub repository search found several such projects, each with fewer than 5 stars.
weaknesses: Target AI authorship, while several major projects explicitly allow AI-assisted work
False positives on legitimate AI-assisted contributions (inference)
Low adoption

competitors.name: Microsoft API Extractor
competitors.description: A TypeScript tool that snapshots a library's public API (.d.ts) so changes can be reviewed, among several other jobs (doc generation, .d.ts rollups).
weaknesses: Heavy setup aimed at larger teams (inference)
Type surface only

competitors.name: cargo-semver-checks (Rust)
competitors.description: Rust's established semver linter with a GitHub Action. It checks a crate's public API before publishing. About 1,700 GitHub stars at retrieval.
weaknesses: Rust only
Documents violations it can't catch

competitors.name: Auto-closing all external pull requests
competitors.description: tldraw closes PRs from external contributors by default and selectively reopens the ones under consideration.
weaknesses: Gives up outside contributions entirely; the maintainer calls it temporary and regrettable

competitors.name: Dependabot cooldown
competitors.description: Delays Dependabot update PRs for newly published versions. GA since July 2025.
strengths: Free on GitHub; adopted mainly for security
weaknesses: Only affects automated update PRs, not manual installs (inference)

competitors.name: Fossier
competitors.description: GitHub Action that scores unknown PR authors on 13 account and content signals (account age, follower ratio, PR description quality…) and auto-allows, flags or closes PRs.
weaknesses: Account-reputation signals penalise genuine newcomers (inference)
Heuristics are gameable (inference)
Small adoption (~41 stars at retrieval)

competitors.name: GitHub pull-request access settings & interaction limits
competitors.description: Native repository controls: disable pull requests, restrict them to collaborators, or apply interaction limits (existing users, prior contributors, collaborators).
weaknesses: Coarse: restricting to collaborators or prior contributors also shuts out legitimate newcomers (inference)
No assessment of contribution quality

competitors.name: npm staged publishing + token-free publishing settings
competitors.description: Opt-in npm features: releases are staged and must be approved by a maintainer with 2FA; a package setting can forbid token publishing; trusted publishers can be limited to staging.
strengths: Free and built into the registry
weaknesses: Opt-in: protects only maintainers who enable it
A human approving a release still has to notice what changed (inference)
Launched May 2026; adoption unknown

competitors.name: pnpm minimumReleaseAge
competitors.description: pnpm setting that refuses to install versions younger than a configured age.
weaknesses: pnpm users only (npm and bun requested it separately)

competitors.name: publint (and arethetypeswrong)
competitors.description: Established linters for npm packaging mistakes (publint, about 1.3k stars) and TypeScript type resolution (arethetypeswrong, about 1.6k stars). They check a single release, not changes between releases.
strengths: Widely known in the JS tooling community
weaknesses: No compare-with-previous-release mode found

competitors.name: PyPI warning when an API token uploads to a trusted-publishing project
competitors.description: An email to maintainers when a long-lived token is used for a project configured for trusted publishing.
strengths: Catches the stolen-token pattern on projects that migrated
weaknesses: Only for projects with trusted publishing configured
No general notice of every new release (none among PyPI's email templates)

competitors.name: Registry trusted publishing (OIDC) on npm and PyPI
competitors.description: Publish from CI using short-lived OIDC identity instead of long-lived tokens.
weaknesses: npm can't use it for a package's first version

competitors.name: Commercial supply-chain scanners (e.g. Socket, StepSecurity)
competitors.description: Vendors that analyse new package releases and publish incident write-ups. Named in the captured issues; their products were not examined in this run.
strengths: Already detect and report incidents quickly (inference from their write-ups being cited)
weaknesses: Not examined in this run

competitors.name: Maintainer triage conventions (autoclose labels, template-compliance rules)
competitors.description: Lightweight project workflows that cut per-PR triage effort: scikit-learn's proposed autoclose label, and nixpkgs' proposal to close PRs that remove the AI-disclosure checkboxes.
strengths: Cheap, transparent, keeps a human in the loop
weaknesses: A human still has to look at each PR to apply the label
Template rules are easy to game (inference)

competitors.name: New TypeScript semver checkers (Clerk break-check, ts-semver-checks, semver-check)
competitors.description: Several 2026 projects that diff the exported TypeScript surface between versions and fail CI on an insufficient version bump. Clerk's is company-backed and uses API Extractor plus an AI review.
weaknesses: Very new; little adoption (0–3 stars at retrieval)
Type surface only: blind to engines, exports and other metadata breaks

competitors.name: Vouch (mitchellh/vouch)
competitors.description: Explicit trust lists: trusted people vouch for contributors, bad actors can be denounced. GitHub Actions integration. Used by Ghostty.
weaknesses: Requires a social path to get vouched (cold start for newcomers, inference)
Public denouncement lists carry governance and abuse risks (inference)
Self-described as experimental

competitors.name: Written AI contribution policies + canned responses
competitors.description: Projects publish AI policies (LLVM, Linux, QEMU, curl, Ghostty, scikit-learn, Zulip, Godot) and close violating PRs with a standard response. LLVM provides a paste-able reply.
strengths: Sets norms and gives maintainers a cheap way to close
weaknesses: Enforcement still requires a human to read each submission
Relies on contributors reading the policy

ideas.title: Adaptive per-dependency cooldown policies
ideas.summary: Recommends a cooldown per dependency based on risk (maintainer count, publish patterns), instead of one fixed delay.
ideas.targetUsers: Teams using Dependabot, Renovate or pnpm cooldowns
ideas.solution: Analyse the dependency graph and suggest per-package cooldown and exclusion lists.

assumptions.text: Teams want fine-grained cooldown controls

risks: Users prefer simple defaults

objections.text: Early adopters overwhelmingly use one simple default delay; fine-grained settings are used by fewer than 10%.

severity.rationale: Delays matter, but a uniform delay already captures most of the benefit.

ideas.statusRationale: Parked. Adoption data shows a preference for simple defaults over fine-grained controls. Revisit if cooldown users report problems with uniform delays.

ideas.title: AI-authorship detector for incoming pull requests
ideas.summary: A GitHub Action that estimates whether a PR was AI-generated, then labels or closes it before a maintainer looks at it.
ideas.solution: Classify PR text and diffs with stylometric and LLM-based detectors, then apply labels, auto-close, or route to a low-priority queue.
ideas.differentiation: Little: several detectors already exist, and they target the same signal.
ideas.feasibility: Easy to build, but AI-text detection is unreliable, and AI-assisted human work is indistinguishable from slop by style alone.

assumptions.text: AI authorship is a good proxy for low-value contributions
Detectors can separate AI from human text with low false-positive rates

risks: Penalises legitimate AI-assisted contributors whom projects explicitly welcome
Arms race with detector evasion

objections.text: Wrong target. Projects mostly accept AI-assisted work: 83.3% of 281 policies permit it, as do Ghostty, curl, Zulip and LLVM. Their objection is to unreviewed, low-understanding work.
Crowded: multiple open-source detectors already exist, and none has meaningful adoption, which suggests weak pull.

severity.rationale: The underlying problem is severe for maintainers (tldraw closed external PRs).

frequency.rationale: Reported across many large projects in 2025–2026.

userValue.rationale: Classifies the wrong attribute, so its value is doubtful.

feasibility.rationale: Easy to ship, hard to make accurate.

userAccess.rationale: Maintainers are easy to reach on GitHub.

validationCost.rationale: Could be validated cheaply on labelled PR data.

ideas.statusRationale: Rejected, and reaffirmed by follow-up evidence. 83.3% of 281 OSS AI policies permit AI in code, so AI authorship is the wrong thing to gate on. The detector space is also crowded.

ideas.title: Comprehension gate for first-time contributors' PRs
ideas.summary: Before a PR from an unknown contributor enters the review queue, its author must answer two or three short, diff-specific questions in their own words. Maintainers see the answers and whether the author engaged at all.
ideas.targetUsers: Maintainers of popular repositories that receive many PRs from first-time contributors
ideas.solution: A GitHub App or Action. When a PR from a non-collaborator without prior merged contributions is opened, it is marked 'awaiting author' and a comment asks diff-specific questions (why this change, what it interacts with, how it was tested). The PR enters the maintainer queue only after the author responds. Follow-up engagement is the primary signal, not detection of AI text. It works alongside vouch lists and GitHub's interaction limits.
ideas.differentiation: It operationalises the requirement that policies already state ('be able to answer questions about their work', 'If you can't explain what your changes do…'). Unlike reputation gates it doesn't exclude newcomers, and unlike detectors it doesn't judge AI use.
ideas.feasibility: High. GitHub webhooks, PR comments and labels are standard. Question generation can start with templates; diff-specific questions would need an LLM (cost to the operator).

assumptions.text: Authors of low-effort PRs rarely respond to maintainer questions, while genuine contributors do (follow-up engagement discriminates)
Maintainers accept a small added delay for newcomers in exchange for a filtered queue
Answers pasted from an LLM still reduce the burden, because they arrive before review time is spent

risks: Authors can paste the questions into an LLM, which weakens the content signal (though not the engagement signal)
Adds friction for legitimate newcomers
GitHub may ship a native equivalent
nextSteps: If it is supported, build a template-only prototype and test it on VENTURE's own repository first

objections.text: An LLM can answer the questions too, so the gate may only add a round-trip for slop authors.
objections.response: The bet is on engagement (does the author respond at all, and quickly), which tldraw reports is typically missing. This is the assumption the experiment tests. Follow-up: in one study of agent PRs, rejections often stemmed from inactivity (indirect support).

objections.text: Friction for genuine newcomers conflicts with projects' stated wish to grow contributors, and newcomers' share of participation is already shrinking where agents are adopted.
objections.response: Questions are short and only apply to authors with no prior merged PRs. Measure newcomer drop-off before adoption.

objections.text: Platform risk: GitHub could add this natively. tldraw explicitly waits for 'better tools' from GitHub.

severity.rationale: Projects are closing external PRs and describe the load as DDoS-like.

frequency.rationale: Reported across many large projects in 2025–2026.

userValue.rationale: Could filter the queue without excluding newcomers. Unproven.

competitiveGap.rationale: Ten countermeasures exist in practice (policy study), but none found gates on comprehension or engagement. Still uncertain.

differentiation.rationale: Aligned with the wording of the policies, but the mechanism is simple to copy.

userAccess.rationale: Maintainers who wrote AI policies are visible on GitHub.

validationCost.rationale: The core assumption can be tested on public GitHub data for $0.

ideas.statusRationale: Parked after a real experiment: follow-up engagement alone separates policy-closed from accepted newcomer PRs only weakly (80.9% vs 90.2% within LLVM), so a reply-required gate would let most low-effort PRs through. Revisit if a cheap way to assess answer content emerges, or if silent closures (33/120) suggest a different intervention.
ideas.noveltyNote: Distinct from AI-authorship detectors (rejected): it gates on author engagement and understanding, not on whether AI was used.

ideas.title: Cross-project contributor reputation registry
ideas.summary: A shared registry where projects publish vouches and denouncements, so trust earned in one project carries over to others.
ideas.solution: Federate vouch-style trust files across projects, with signed attestations and a lookup API used by gating Actions.
ideas.differentiation: Network effects across projects. Vouch already allows lists to be shared, so differentiation is thin.
ideas.feasibility: Technically simple, socially and legally hard.

assumptions.text: Projects are willing to trust other projects' vouches
Public denouncements can be governed without abuse or defamation risk

risks: Public blacklists invite brigading, mistaken identity and legal risk
Vouch may grow into this itself
nextSteps: Revisit if Vouch adoption grows and projects start importing each other's lists

objections.text: Governance and abuse risks of a shared public denouncement list outweigh the benefit for a small team to operate.
The incumbent (Vouch, ~5k stars, Ghostty) is positioned to add federation itself.

severity.rationale: Trust breakdown is real but indirect.

frequency.rationale: Affects many projects, but few have adopted explicit trust lists yet.

differentiation.rationale: Federation is a feature, not a product.

validationCost.rationale: Hard to test without network adoption.

ideas.statusRationale: Reconsidered after new evidence on the trust-signal problem (newcomer share declines 3.7 points after agent adoption). The problem looks more real, but the main objections (governance and abuse risk of shared denouncement lists, incumbent Vouch) are unaffected. Stays parked.

ideas.title: Downstream dependent test runner ('crater for npm')
ideas.summary: Before releasing, run the test suites of a sample of the package's dependents against the release candidate, to catch behaviour breaks that static checks miss.
ideas.targetUsers: Maintainers of widely used npm packages
ideas.solution: A service that picks dependents with test suites, installs the release candidate in their place, runs their tests, and reports regressions.
ideas.differentiation: Catches behaviour breaks like React 16.4's, which no static tool can.
ideas.feasibility: Hard: arbitrary test suites need sandboxed execution, and the compute cost is significant.

assumptions.text: Enough dependents have runnable test suites

risks: Running untrusted dependents' code
Compute cost
Flaky dependents' tests create noise

objections.text: Running thousands of untrusted test suites safely is expensive and complex. It's not something VENTURE can build or run for free.

severity.rationale: Behaviour breaks are the hardest to catch.

competitiveGap.rationale: Not found for npm; not searched exhaustively.

ideas.statusRationale: Parked. Potentially valuable, but expensive and risky to run (executing untrusted code at scale), and well beyond what VENTURE can build for free.

practical.smallestUsefulVersion: A GitHub Action that runs the tests of 10 hand-picked dependents against a release candidate.
practical.buildNote: Needs sandboxed execution of untrusted code and paid compute.
practical.monetization: Possible as a hosted service for large maintainers or companies, but costly to operate.

ideas.title: Publish-anomaly alarm for maintainers
ideas.summary: Watches the registry for new versions of a maintainer's own packages and alerts within minutes if a release differs structurally from the maintainer's normal releases.
ideas.targetUsers: Maintainers of widely used packages without a security team
ideas.solution: Subscribe to registry publish events for owned packages. Diff each release against the previous one for structural anomalies: newly added dependencies, new install-time hooks or .pth files, publishing outside the usual CI identity, missing provenance. Notify the maintainer through an out-of-band channel they control.
ideas.differentiation: Maintainer-side and owner-verified: the maintainer can say 'that wasn't me' fastest. Vendors protect consumers after analysis.
ideas.feasibility: Registry metadata and tarballs are public. The anomaly rules are simple diffs.

assumptions.text: Malicious releases from compromised accounts differ structurally (new deps, new hooks, different publisher) from the maintainer's normal releases
Maintainers would notice and react faster than the current detection time (~3 h for axios)
Commercial scanners don't already offer free maintainer-side alerts
A substantial share of popular packages still publish in a way a stolen token could reproduce (no trusted publishing, no staged approval)

risks: An attacker who controls the account may also control the notification channel
Vendors may already cover this (not examined)
False positives on legitimate dependency changes
nextSteps: If the gap is real, consider a review aid for staged releases that highlights new install hooks at approval time

objections.text: Commercial scanners (Socket, StepSecurity) already analyse new releases quickly. The marginal value of maintainer-side alerts is unproven.
If the attacker controls the maintainer's account or email, alerts may be intercepted.
objections.response: Use a channel registered independently of the registry account.

objections.text: Some attacks, like asyncapi's branch-token compromise, publish through the normal CI pipeline, so publisher-identity checks wouldn't fire.

npm now offers prevention to maintainers who opt in (staged publishing with 2FA approval, token-free publishing), and PyPI warns about token uploads to trusted-publishing projects. The alarm only adds value for maintainers who haven't adopted these.
objections.response: Measure adoption: if most popular packages still publish without these protections, the alarm's audience remains large (exp-npm-publishing-practices).

severity.rationale: RATs and credential stealers in packages with huge reach.

frequency.rationale: Several high-profile incidents in 2026 in the captured signals.

userValue.rationale: Could cut exposure windows, if anomalies are detectable.

competitiveGap.rationale: Vendors exist; maintainer-side free alerts not verified either way.

validationCost.rationale: Can be checked retrospectively on public registry data for $0.

ideas.statusRationale: Stays advanced. The technical premise (most hijacks add install hooks) and the audience (about half of popular packages still publish without npm's new protections, including most previously hijacked ones) are both supported by pre-registered experiments. Remaining unknowns: whether maintainers want such alerts and act on them, and whether vendors already offer them.

practical.adopters: Maintainers of npm packages, especially those not using trusted publishing or staged approval (about half of popular packages)
practical.smallestUsefulVersion: A GitHub Action or small service that watches your own packages on npm and alerts you when a new release adds an install script or an unexpected dependency.
practical.buildNote: The same registry diffing VENTURE already runs daily in the install-hook watch.
practical.monetization: Mainly as a free open-source tool. Security vendors and npm itself are moving into this space, so a paid product is unlikely.

ideas.title: Release-contract linter for npm packages
ideas.summary: Before publishing, check the parts of a release's contract that type checkers ignore: engine requirements tightened, entry points or exports paths removed, module format switched, new required peer dependencies, removed CLI commands. Fail if a minor or patch release changes them.
ideas.targetUsers: Maintainers of JavaScript and TypeScript packages on npm (including packages without types)
ideas.solution: A CLI and GitHub Action that compares the package.json and published file list of the release candidate with the last published version on npm, and flags contract changes that need a major bump (engines.node raised, exports subpaths removed or an exports map added, main/module/types removed, type: module switch, new non-optional peer dependencies, bin entries removed). It can run alongside a type-surface checker.
ideas.differentiation: Existing tools inspect the TypeScript type surface. This inspects the install- and import-time contract, which breaks even for untyped packages (e.g. polished's engines bump). It complements the type checkers rather than replacing them.
ideas.feasibility: High. Everything needed is in package.json and the npm registry metadata. No compiler work is needed.

assumptions.text: Metadata-level contract breaks in minor or patch releases are common among popular packages (≥ 20% shipped at least one in two years)
Flags are mostly genuine breaks rather than noise (≥ 70% of audited flags)
Maintainers would add another check to their release workflow

risks: The rules may be too strict (some engines bumps are deliberate and announced)
Existing checkers may add metadata rules
Behaviour breaks (React 16.4) remain invisible
nextSteps: If supported, build the CLI and dogfood it on real packages

objections.text: Behaviour changes, like React 16.4's, are invisible to any static check, so this catches only part of the problem.
objections.response: It doesn't need to catch everything to be useful. The experiment measures how much it catches.

objections.text: Some maintainers deliberately tighten engines in minor releases (e.g. dropping end-of-life Node). They may consider that acceptable, and see the linter as noise.
objections.response: The audit step measures how many flags are genuine. Rules can be configured.

objections.text: The type-checker projects could add metadata rules quickly.
Engine-range rules dominate the flags and are mostly debatable (dropping end-of-life Node), which made 60% of audited flags non-genuine.
objections.response: A narrowed, structural-only rule set was 78% precise in the audit (exploratory), but fires for only about 10% of popular packages.

severity.rationale: Breaking minor releases cost users real time.

frequency.rationale: Frequency of metadata breaks unknown; being measured.

userValue.rationale: Catches a class of breaks no current tool checks, before publish.

competitiveGap.rationale: No tool found that checks the install/import contract.

userAccess.rationale: Maintainers reachable via GitHub Marketplace and npm.

validationCost.rationale: Frequency testable for $0 on registry data.

ideas.statusRationale: Parked with a narrowed recommendation. As specified, the linter is too noisy (40% genuine). A structural-only rule set looks precise (about 78% in a small exploratory sample) but helps only about 1 in 10 popular packages. Its practical value is as a 'compare with last release' feature for an existing linter like publint, pending validation on a fresh sample.
ideas.noveltyNote: Distinct from the rejected type-surface checker: it inspects package metadata and the published file contract, not .d.ts types.

practical.adopters: npm package maintainers, as a pre-publish check, and possibly downstream teams auditing updates
practical.smallestUsefulVersion: A 'compare with last release' mode for publint (or a small plugin) with the structural rules: removed export paths, entry fields, CLI commands and peer tightening. Engine checks only if they know Node's end-of-life dates.
practical.buildNote: Needs only package.json parsing, npm registry metadata and the semver library. VENTURE already uses all three.
practical.monetization: None realistic: best as an upstream contribution to existing open-source linters.

ideas.title: Reproduction-first triage for AI-assisted security reports
ideas.summary: Security reports must include a proof of concept that a sandboxed CI job runs against the released code before any human reads the report.
ideas.targetUsers: Security teams of widely used open-source projects
ideas.solution: An intake form and a sandboxed runner execute the submitted PoC against pinned releases and attach the result. Reports that don't reproduce go to a low-priority queue.
ideas.differentiation: Shifts verification cost back to the reporter mechanically.
ideas.feasibility: Possible, but it requires executing untrusted code safely, and many real vulnerabilities (logic bugs, race conditions, memory corruption needing special builds) are hard to demonstrate in a generic sandbox.

assumptions.text: Most valid reports can include a mechanically runnable PoC

risks: Running attacker-supplied code
Raises the bar for legitimate reporters
Bug-bounty platforms may already offer triage services (not researched in this run)
nextSteps: Gather more independent evidence on report volumes. Secondary sources were blocked in this session.

objections.text: Evidence is thin: only one independent origin (curl) was retrievable in this session.
Executing untrusted PoCs is itself a security risk, and many genuine findings can't be reproduced generically.

severity.rationale: curl ended its bug bounty and describes fake reports as blocking real work.

frequency.rationale: Only one origin evidenced in this run.

userValue.rationale: High if it works, but many reports can't be auto-reproduced.

competitiveGap.rationale: Platform triage services were not investigated, so this score is uncertain.

feasibility.rationale: Sandboxing and generic reproduction are hard.

userAccess.rationale: Security teams are reachable but cautious.

validationCost.rationale: Could be tested on historical public advisories.

ideas.statusRationale: Parked for insufficient evidence. Only curl's own documents were retrievable, so news coverage and platform alternatives are unexamined. Revisit with broader sources.

ideas.title: Standalone release-age cooldown tool for all package managers
ideas.summary: A wrapper or proxy that blocks installing package versions younger than N days, for ecosystems whose package managers don't support it yet.
ideas.solution: A registry proxy or install wrapper that filters out versions published within the last N days, with an allowlist for urgent fixes.
ideas.differentiation: Covers package managers that haven't shipped the feature yet.
ideas.feasibility: Simple to build: registry metadata includes publish times.

assumptions.text: Package managers will be slow to ship native release-age settings

risks: Platform features make it obsolete
Delays urgent security fixes

objections.text: pnpm and Dependabot already ship cooldowns, and npm and bun have popular open requests. A standalone tool competes with imminent free platform features.

severity.rationale: Account compromises shipped RATs and credential stealers.

competitiveGap.rationale: Free platform features exist or are requested upstream.

ideas.statusRationale: Rejected. Release-age delays are already being solved by the platforms themselves (pnpm, Dependabot; npm and bun requests open). There's no durable gap for a standalone tool.

ideas.title: TypeScript API-surface semver checker
ideas.summary: A 'cargo-semver-checks for TypeScript': diff the exported .d.ts surface between the last release and the next, and fail CI if the version bump understates the change.
ideas.targetUsers: Maintainers of TypeScript libraries on npm
ideas.solution: Generate API snapshots from .d.ts files, classify each change as major, minor or patch, and compare with the planned version bump in a CLI and GitHub Action.
ideas.differentiation: None that's clear: at least three 2026 projects and Microsoft's API Extractor already do this.
ideas.feasibility: Feasible: the TypeScript compiler API exposes the surface.

assumptions.text: Most accidental breaking releases are type-surface changes

risks: A crowded niche
Misses behaviour and metadata breaks

objections.text: Already being built by at least three projects, one company-backed (Clerk), on top of Microsoft's API Extractor.
None of the four real breakage complaints examined (React, node-abort-controller, floating-ui, polished) was a type-surface change, so the approach misses many real breaks.

severity.rationale: Breaking minor releases cost users real time (weekends, pinned versions).

frequency.rationale: Hundreds of issues titled about it; true frequency not yet measured.

ideas.statusRationale: Rejected. The TypeScript type-surface checker niche is already being filled (Clerk's break-check, ts-semver-checks, semver-check, API Extractor), and the real complaints examined weren't type-surface breaks.

practical.smallestUsefulVersion: A CLI and GitHub Action that diffs .d.ts exports between versions.
practical.buildNote: Straightforward with the TypeScript compiler API.
practical.monetization: Unlikely: several free tools already exist.

ideas.title: Validated pre-review triage signals for maintainers
ideas.summary: A suggestion-only ranking of incoming PRs, so maintainers can triage the likely low-effort ones first. It uses only signals shown to separate low-effort from genuine contributions before anyone reads the code.
ideas.targetUsers: Maintainers of popular repositories with many first-time PRs
ideas.solution: A GitHub Action that, for each PR from a first-time contributor, computes a few cheap signals available before review (e.g. the author's recent PR burst across GitHub, account age, template compliance) and labels the PR with a triage priority and the reasons. It never closes PRs itself; maintainers decide.
ideas.differentiation: Existing tools (Fossier) combine many signals with hand-set weights that haven't been validated, and close PRs automatically. This would use only signals with measured discrimination, and stay advisory, keeping humans in the decision (see the disparate-impact objection to blunt policies).
ideas.feasibility: High: the signals come from public GitHub APIs.

assumptions.text: Cheap pre-review signals (recent cross-repo PR burst, account age) separate policy-violating PRs from genuine newcomer PRs well (AUC ≥ 0.75)
Advisory labels save maintainers meaningful triage time
Signals don't systematically disadvantage genuine newcomers (e.g. new accounts)

risks: Account-age signals penalise genuine newcomers
Spammers adapt once signals are known
Fossier already ships similar signals

objections.text: Fossier already scores unknown contributors on 13 signals, including open PRs elsewhere and account age. Differentiation rests only on validation and advisory mode.
Account-based signals can exclude genuine newcomers and contributors who use AI as assistive technology, the same disparate-impact concern raised against blunt policies.
objections.response: Advisory only, and the experiment reports how many genuine newcomers each signal would flag.

objections.text: Even a ranked queue still needs a human to look at each PR. The saving may be small.

severity.rationale: Triage cost is closing newcomer on-ramps (Astropy) and prompting autoclose workflows.

userValue.rationale: Depends on how well the signals discriminate; unknown.

competitiveGap.rationale: Fossier covers similar ground without validation.

differentiation.rationale: Validation plus an advisory design; thin.

userAccess.rationale: Maintainers who wrote AI policies are reachable on GitHub.

validationCost.rationale: Signal discrimination is testable on existing labelled data for $0.

ideas.statusRationale: Rejected. Across three pre-registered tests, no cheap pre-review signal or simple combination separates policy-violating PRs from genuine newcomer PRs well enough (best AUC 0.67-0.69) without flagging many genuine newcomers. The same evidence suggests that tools built on these signals (e.g. Fossier) are unlikely to triage reliably.
ideas.noveltyNote: Distinct from the parked comprehension gate (which relied on post-submission engagement): this uses signals available before any interaction.

experiments.title: Do two partial signals combined (description length + recent cross-repo PR count) separate policy-violating PRs well?
experiments.hypothesis: An unfitted, equal-weight combination of description length (C2) and the author's recent cross-repo PR count (S1) reaches AUC ≥ 0.75 on the same 240 labelled PRs.
experiments.uncertainty: Whether the two partially informative cheap signals add up to a usable triage signal. This is the last cheap test before pausing the area's solution search.
procedure: Pre-registered 2026-11-04. The individual signals were measured earlier (S1 AUC 0.64, C2 AUC 0.67); this combination and its rule are fixed before measuring them together.
Sample: the same 240 PRs. Re-collect S1 (search API, 30 days before the PR) and C2 (description word count) per PR.
Score = (percentile rank of C2 among all PRs + percentile rank of S1 among all PRs) / 2. No weights are fitted.
Primary: AUC of the score. Also report the newcomer flag rate at the threshold that flags half of the policy-closed PRs.
successCriteria: Combined AUC ≥ 0.75 over at least 150 PRs
failureCriteria: Combined AUC < 0.70: pause the area's solution search
resources: GitHub REST and search APIs via the Actions token
experiments.expectedLearning: Whether cheap signals can support triage at all, or whether the area should stop looking for a solution of this kind.

nextSteps.ifSuccess: Validate on a second, non-LLVM control group before reopening the idea.
nextSteps.ifFailure: Pause the solution search in this area, and record the negative result as the area's main contribution.

outcome.summary: Pre-registered verdict: refuted. An unfitted equal-weight combination of description length and recent cross-repo PR count reached AUC 0.69, just below the 0.70 line, and would flag about 25% of genuine newcomers at half recall (worse than description length alone, about 13%). The threshold isn't moved after seeing the result.

experiments.title: Do content-based signals in the PR itself separate policy-violating PRs from genuine newcomer PRs?
experiments.hypothesis: PRs closed under AI or low-effort policies differ from merged first-time LLVM PRs in cheap content signals visible before review: whether the description links an existing issue (C1), and description length (C2). At least one reaches AUC ≥ 0.75.
experiments.uncertainty: Whether any cheap pre-review signal works, now that account-level signals have failed. If content signals fail too, the area should be paused.
procedure: Pre-registered 2026-11-04 before any content data was collected.
Sample: the 240 PRs from exp-followup-engagement-retrospective (120 policy-closed, 120 merged LLVM newcomer PRs). Labels are already known.
For each PR, read the description (body) via the GitHub REST API. It may have been edited after closing, a limitation.
C1: does the description reference an issue (#number, or a GitHub issue URL)? Absence → more suspicious.
C2: description length in words. Direction not assumed: AUC is reported as max(AUC, 1−AUC), with the observed direction stated.
Primary: the better of C1 and C2 by AUC. Also report the share of genuine newcomers flagged at the threshold that flags half the policy-closed PRs.
successCriteria: The better content signal reaches AUC ≥ 0.75 over at least 150 PRs with readable descriptions
failureCriteria: Both content signals have AUC < 0.60 (pause the area's solution search)
resources: GitHub REST API via the Actions token
experiments.expectedLearning: Whether triage support can be built on what a PR says, after account-level signals failed.

nextSteps.ifSuccess: Reopen the triage-signal idea with content signals and test them on a second, non-LLVM control group.
nextSteps.ifFailure: Pause the solution search in this area, and record that cheap pre-review signals don't separate low-effort from genuine PRs.

outcome.summary: Pre-registered verdict: inconclusive. Issue references don't discriminate (AUC 0.51). Description length does moderately (AUC 0.67; median 166 vs 87 words, longer for policy-violating PRs), flagging about 13% of genuine newcomers at half recall.

experiments.title: Does author follow-up engagement separate policy-rejected PRs from accepted first-time PRs?
experiments.hypothesis: Authors of PRs that projects closed as low-effort or AI-policy violations rarely reply to maintainer comments, while first-time contributors whose PRs were merged usually do.
experiments.uncertainty: Whether follow-up engagement is a discriminating signal (assumption a1). If it isn't, a comprehension gate adds friction without filtering.
procedure: Pre-registered 2026-11-03, before any outcome data was collected. Revised from the original per-repo design because GitHub search showed only 10 LLVM PRs citing the policy.

Group A (policy-closed): closed, unmerged PRs created 2025-06-01..2026-11-01 whose text or comments cite an AI policy ('AIToolPolicy', 'policy on tool-generated content', 'AI_POLICY.md', or 'AI slop' in comments), pooled across GitHub, up to 120 PRs.
Group B (newcomer-merged): merged llvm/llvm-project PRs from the same period that received LLVM's first-time-contributor greeting, up to 120.
Group C (newcomer-closed, descriptive only): unmerged LLVM newcomer PRs not citing the policy.

For each PR, fetch issue and review comments via the GitHub REST API. Among PRs with at least one comment by a human other than the author (bots excluded), record whether the author replied afterwards, and the time to reply.
Compare reply rates (Wilson 95% intervals) and median reply times. Code: src/experiments/followup-engagement.ts; runs in the 'Run experiment' workflow.
successCriteria: Group A reply rate is at most half of group B's, with at least 30 eligible PRs in each group
failureCriteria: Reply rates of A and B differ by less than 15 percentage points (assumption refuted)
Fewer than 30 eligible PRs in either group (inconclusive)
resources: GitHub REST and search APIs via the Actions GITHUB_TOKEN
experiments.expectedLearning: Whether engagement-based gating is worth prototyping, and how much newcomer friction it would cause (via the reply-time distribution of genuine contributors).

nextSteps.ifSuccess: Build a template-question prototype and dogfood it on this repository. Only contact other maintainers with owner approval.
nextSteps.ifFailure: Mark assumption a1 refuted and reject or park the idea. Look for other discriminating signals.

outcome.summary: Pre-registered verdict: inconclusive. Policy-closed PR authors replied 59.8% of the time (52/87, CI 49–69%) versus 90.2% for merged LLVM newcomers (83/92, CI 82–95%): a clear gap, but short of the ≤ 45.1% success threshold. Exploratory within-LLVM comparison: 80.9% vs 90.2%, so engagement alone discriminates weakly.

experiments.title: Prospective field test: how often would the alarm fire on real releases?
experiments.hypothesis: Across the 400 popular npm packages from exp-npm-publishing-practices, new releases that add an install script or a new dependency are rare enough (≤ 5% of releases) that alerts wouldn't overwhelm maintainers.
experiments.uncertainty: Real-world alert volume (false-alarm burden), which retrospective data on malicious releases can't show.
procedure: Pre-registered 2026-11-04 before any monitoring data was collected.
Daily for 28 days, a scheduled workflow lists new versions of the 400 packages published since the previous check (public npm registry).
For each new version, compare with the previous version: install scripts added or changed, new dependencies.
After 28 days, cross-check flagged versions against OpenSSF malicious-packages reports.
Report the alert rate per release and per package-month, and the number of confirmed malicious hits.
successCriteria: At most 5% of new releases trigger an alert, over at least 300 observed releases
failureCriteria: More than 15% of new releases trigger an alert (alert fatigue likely)
experiments.expectedLearning: The false-alarm burden in practice. Malicious hits are unlikely in 28 days, so absence of hits is expected and not evidence against the idea.

nextSteps.ifSuccess: Ask the owner to authorize a small maintainer interest test (requires contacting people).
nextSteps.ifFailure: Refine the signal (e.g. only install hooks) before any further work.

experiments.title: How often do popular npm packages ship metadata-level breaking changes in minor or patch releases?
experiments.hypothesis: At least 20% of popular npm packages shipped at least one minor or patch release in the past 24 months that a release-contract linter would flag. At least 70% of a random sample of flags are genuine breaking changes.
experiments.uncertainty: Whether the problem the linter targets is common enough (assumption a1), and whether its flags would be trusted (assumption a2).
procedure: Pre-registered 2026-11-04 before any release data was collected.
Population: the 400 popular npm packages from exp-npm-publishing-practices.
For each package, take consecutive non-prerelease versions published in the 24 months before 2026-11-04, keeping pairs where the later one is a minor or patch bump of the earlier.

Rules (from registry metadata): engines.node minimum raised; exports subpath removed, or an exports map added where none existed; main, module, types or typings removed; type switched to module; a new non-optional peer dependency added, or an existing peer's minimum major raised; a bin entry removed.
Report the share of packages with at least one flagged release, the share of release pairs flagged, and counts per rule.
Audit: a research session reviews 20 randomly sampled flags (fixed seed) and judges each as a genuine break per SemVer or not, documenting reasons.
successCriteria: At least 20% of packages have at least one flagged minor or patch release in the window, and at least 70% of the 20 audited flags are genuine breaks
failureCriteria: Fewer than 5% of packages have a flagged release (the problem is too rare to justify a tool)
Fewer than 50% of audited flags are genuine (too noisy)
experiments.estimatedTime: < 1 hour of automated analysis plus a manual audit of 20 flags
experiments.expectedLearning: Whether a release-contract linter would catch a meaningful number of real breaks with acceptable noise, before anything is built.

nextSteps.ifSuccess: Build the CLI and GitHub Action, and dogfood it by running it over recent releases of popular packages.
nextSteps.ifFailure: Reject or narrow the idea to the rules that proved common and precise.

outcome.summary: Pre-registered verdict: refuted. The frequency criterion was met exactly (80 of 400 popular packages, 20.0%), but only 8 of 20 audited flags were genuine breaks (40%, below the 50% failure line). Most noise came from engine-range rules dropping end-of-life Node versions. Exploratory: structural rules alone were genuine in 7 of 9 audited cases, but flag only about 10% of packages.

experiments.title: How many popular npm packages still publish in a way a stolen token could reproduce?
experiments.hypothesis: A substantial share (≥ 40%) of popular npm packages' latest releases were published with neither trusted publishing (OIDC) nor staged human approval, so a maintainer-side alarm would still have a large audience.
experiments.uncertainty: Whether npm's new protections have already closed most of the gap the alarm targets (assumption a4).
procedure: Pre-registered 2026-11-04 before data collection. A metadata probe of one package (axios) confirmed the fields exist.

Population A (popular): union of the top 250 results of the npm search API (popularity weight 1.0) for the keywords javascript, typescript, react, node, cli and util. Deduplicated, first 400 packages in result order.
Population B (previously hijacked): the 22 campaign-representative packages from exp-publish-anomaly-campaign-replication.
For each package's latest version, read `_npmUser` from the registry: `trustedPublisher` present → OIDC; `approver` present → staged with human approval; neither → token/interactive publish.
Report the shares, with Wilson 95% intervals.
successCriteria: At least 40% of population A's latest releases have neither trusted publishing nor staged approval (the alarm still has a large audience)
failureCriteria: Fewer than 15% have neither (npm's protections already cover most popular packages)
Fewer than 200 packages could be read (inconclusive)
resources: Public npm registry and search API
experiments.expectedLearning: How much of the popular npm ecosystem is still exposed to the token-theft route that hit axios, and whether previously hijacked packages changed their publishing after the attack.

nextSteps.ifSuccess: Refine the alarm toward the exposed population, and consider a staged-release review aid that highlights new install hooks at approval time.
nextSteps.ifFailure: Park the standalone alarm. npm's own controls cover most of its audience.

outcome.summary: Pre-registered verdict: supported. 201 of 400 popular npm packages (50.2%, 95% CI 45–55%) published their latest release with neither trusted publishing nor staged approval. Only 31 (7.8%) use staged human approval. 13 of 22 previously hijacked packages still publish with neither. 'Neither' is an upper bound, because interactive 2FA publishes look the same in metadata.

experiments.title: Do cheap pre-review signals separate policy-violating PRs from genuine newcomer PRs?
experiments.hypothesis: Authors of PRs closed under AI or low-effort policies opened many more PRs across GitHub in the 30 days before their PR than genuine first-time LLVM contributors did, so this one signal separates the groups well (AUC ≥ 0.75).
experiments.uncertainty: Whether any cheap, pre-review signal discriminates at all (assumption a1).
procedure: Pre-registered 2026-11-04 before any signal data was collected.
Sample: the 240 PRs from exp-followup-engagement-retrospective (120 policy-closed, 120 merged LLVM newcomer PRs). Labels are already known.
For each PR, read its creation time (GitHub REST API).
Signal S1: number of PRs the author opened across GitHub in the 30 days before the PR (search API, type:pr author:<login> created:<range>).
Signal S2: author account age at PR creation, in days (users API).
Authors whose accounts no longer exist are counted and reported separately, and excluded from the AUC.
Primary: AUC of S1 (higher → policy-closed). Secondary: AUC of S2 (younger → policy-closed). Secondary: S1 AUC within LLVM only.
Report the share of genuine newcomers flagged at the threshold that catches 50% of policy-closed PRs.
successCriteria: S1 AUC ≥ 0.75 over at least 150 PRs with readable authors
failureCriteria: Both S1 and S2 have AUC < 0.60 (cheap signals don't discriminate)
Fewer than 150 PRs with readable authors (inconclusive)
resources: GitHub REST and search APIs via the Actions token
experiments.expectedLearning: Whether pre-review triage support (and tools like Fossier) rests on signals that work, and what they would cost genuine newcomers.

nextSteps.ifSuccess: Prototype an advisory triage Action on this repository's own PRs. Any outreach to other projects needs owner authorization.
nextSteps.ifFailure: Reject this idea and note that unvalidated signal-based tools (Fossier) are likely ineffective.

outcome.summary: Pre-registered verdict: inconclusive. The cross-repo PR burst separates the groups only weakly (AUC 0.64; median 6 vs 1 prior PRs), and account age barely at all (AUC 0.54). Catching half of the policy-violating PRs would also flag about 30% of genuine newcomers. Cheap account-level signals aren't a good basis for triage.

experiments.title: Campaign-level replication: do independent hijack campaigns carry structural signals?
experiments.hypothesis: Across independent npm hijack campaigns (not individual packages), most carry a new-dependency or install-hook signal.
experiments.uncertainty: Whether the first experiment's support generalises beyond the single Shai-Hulud wave that dominated its sample.
procedure: Pre-registered 2026-11-03, before any campaign-level data collection.
Population: OpenSSF OSV reports 2024-01-01..2026-11-02 for hijacked legitimate npm packages (at least 10 non-malicious versions).
Group incidents into campaigns: same campaign name in the report, or same publish date and payload description. Take one representative per campaign.
Classify each campaign's mechanism as in exp-publish-anomaly-retrospective. Reuse the same false-positive baseline method.
successCriteria: At least 60% of classifiable campaigns carry a new-dependency or install-hook signal, with at least 15 classifiable campaigns
failureCriteria: Fewer than 40% of classifiable campaigns carry such signals
experiments.estimatedTime: half a day of automated analysis
experiments.expectedLearning: Whether structural diffing generalises across attackers, or only catches worm-style campaigns.

nextSteps.ifSuccess: Survey vendor offerings for maintainer-side alerts, then prototype on VENTURE's own packages (none yet).
nextSteps.ifFailure: Narrow the idea to worm/install-hook detection or park it.

outcome.summary: Pre-registered verdict: supported. 12 of 15 classifiable independent campaigns (80%, 95% CI 55–93%) added an install-time hook, versus 1.7% of 423 legitimate releases. Caveats: exactly the minimum of 15 classifiable campaigns; 7 campaigns of unknown mechanism (the share could range from 55% to 86%); 3 file-modification campaigns would evade the alarm.

experiments.title: Would simple structural diffs have flagged the documented malicious releases?
experiments.hypothesis: Each documented malicious release differs from the previous legitimate release by at least one simple structural signal: a new dependency, a new install-time hook or .pth file, or a missing or changed provenance attestation.
experiments.uncertainty: Whether compromised-account releases are structurally anomalous (assumption a1). If they look like normal releases, a maintainer alarm can't work.
procedure: Pre-registered before data collection; revised after a metadata-only feasibility probe.

Feasibility probe (2026-11-03T22:46Z): the malicious versions have been removed from npm and PyPI. Archive source: OpenSSF malicious-packages (OSV) reports, which describe the injected mechanism per malicious version (e.g. MAL-2026-2307 axios, MAL-2026-2144 litellm, MAL-2025-190643 @asyncapi/specs).

Population: OSV entries from 2025-06-01 to 2026-11-01 for packages that still have at least 10 non-malicious versions on their registry (hijacked legitimate packages, not typosquats), up to 60 incidents.
Classify each incident's mechanism from the OSV text into: new dependency, new install-time script or hook (.pth, pre/postinstall), modification of existing files only, or unknown.
False positives: for the same npm packages, use public per-version registry metadata to count how often consecutive legitimate releases add a dependency or an install script.
Code goes under src/experiments/ and runs in the 'Run experiment' workflow; raw results are committed under research/experiments/.
successCriteria: At least 60% of classifiable incidents involve a new dependency or install-time hook
Fewer than 10% of legitimate npm releases add a dependency or install script
failureCriteria: Fewer than 40% of classifiable incidents involve such signals (most attacks only modify existing files)
experiments.estimatedTime: half a day of automated analysis
resources: Public npm and PyPI registry APIs
experiments.expectedLearning: Whether structural anomaly detection is a viable basis for maintainer-side alerts, and its false-positive cost.

nextSteps.ifSuccess: Survey existing vendor offerings for maintainer-side alerts before prototyping.
nextSteps.ifFailure: Reject or park the alarm; investigate behaviour-based detection instead.

outcome.summary: Pre-registered verdict: supported. 58/58 classifiable hijack incidents carried an install-hook signal (95% CI 94–100%), versus 1.3% of 1,119 legitimate releases. Caveat from the independence check: 56 of 60 incidents belong to one Shai-Hulud campaign wave, so this is about 5 independent attacks. Assumption a1 stays untested pending a campaign-level replication (pre-registered).

signals.title: The Quiet Contributions: Insights into AI-Generated Silent Pull Requests
signals.excerpt: We present the first empirical study of AI-generated pull requests that are 'silent,' meaning no comments or discussions accompany them. This absence of any comments or discussions associated with such silent AI pull requests (SPRs) poses a unique challenge in understanding the rationale for their acceptance or rejection. Hence, we quantitatively study 4,762 SPRs of five AI agents made to popular Python repositories drawn from the AIDev public dataset. We examine SPRs impact on code complexity, other quality issues, and security vulnerabilities, especially to determine whether these insights can hint at the rationale for acceptance or rejection of SPRs.

signals.title: A Task-Level Evaluation of AI Agents in Open-Source Projects
signals.excerpt: In this paper, we present a comparative study of five autonomous coding agents using AIDev-pop, which is a public dataset containing thousands of AI-generated pull requests (PRs) across popular open-source repositories. We evaluate agents' performance along three task-aware dimensions spanning the PR lifecycle: (1) PR acceptance rate, (2) review discussion volume, and (3) commit message quality. Our quantitative analysis finds that Codex consistently achieves high PR acceptance rates across most task categories, while Copilot's PRs trigger the highest volume of both human and automated review discussions. In contrast, commit-level quality varies independently of acceptance outcomes. Claude and Cursor produce higher proportions of high-quality commit messages across several task types, and Codex exhibiting comparatively lower commit quality despite strong integration outcomes. Our findings inform selection and improvements of AI agents for their effective integration to collaborative software engineering.

signals.title: Insights into Security-Related AI-Generated Pull Requests
signals.excerpt: Recent years have experienced growing contributions of AI coding agents that assist human developers in various software engineering tasks. However, this growing AI-assisted autonomy raises questions about security and trust. In this paper, we analyze more than 33,000 AI-generated pull requests (PRs) and identify 675 security-related submissions made by agentic AIs. Then we examine the security-related PRs with a focus on recurring security weaknesses, review outcomes and latency, commit message quality, and rejection reasons. The results show that security-related AI PRs introduce a small set of recurring weaknesses such as regex inefficiencies, injection flaws, and path traversal. Many flawed contributions are still merged, while rejections often arise from social or process factors such as inactivity or missing test coverage. The commit message quality of AI PRs has a limited effect on acceptance or latency, in contrast to human PRs reported in previous studies. We also extend existing rejection taxonomies by adding categories that are unique to AI-generated security contributions. signals.title: These Aren't the Reviews You're Looking For How Humans Review AI-Generated Pull Requests
signals.excerpt: We analyze code review interactions for AI-generated pull requests (PRs) on GitHub using the AIDev dataset and compare them to human-authored PRs within the same repositories. We find that most AI-generated PRs receive no review and, when reviewed, are largely dominated by AI agents rather than humans. Human-authored PRs are more likely to receive human-only review and to attract direct human feedback. In contrast, reviews of AI-generated PRs more often take the form of automation-mediated interaction, with human involvement frequently expressed through agent steering rather than standalone evaluation. These results indicate systematic differences in how review activity is structured in agentic workflows and raise challenges for interpreting review metrics as indicators of human oversight in large-scale mining studies.

signals.title: To What Extent Does Agent-generated Code Require Maintenance? An Empirical Study
signals.excerpt: LLM-based autonomous coding agents have reshaped software development. While these agents excel at code generation, open questions persist about the long-term maintainability of AI-generated code. This study empirically investigates the maintenance extent, human involvement, and modification types of AI-generated files versus human-authored code. Using the AIDev dataset of AI-generated pull requests and GitHub, we analyzed over 1,000 files and approximately 3,200 changes from 100 popular repositories. Our findings show that: (i) AI-generated files receive less frequent maintenance than human-authored code, with updates affecting only a small fraction of file size; (ii) the most frequent modifications to AI code are feature extensions, whereas human updates focus on bug fixes, and (iii) human developers perform the large majority of this maintenance.

signals.title: Supply chain risk in init command: unverified remote code fetching
signals.excerpt: The `init` command in `browser_use/init_cmd.py` fetches Python template files from `raw.githubusercontent.com` at runtime and writes them to disk for execution. There's no integrity verification — no checksum, no signature, no pinned commit. **What happens:** 1. `_fetch_template_list()` downloads `templates.json` from `browser-use/template-library` (line 37) 2. `_fetch_from_github()` downloads the actual Python file content 3. Content is written to disk and the user is told to run `python {output_path.name}` If the `template-library` repo is compromised (via a maintainer account takeover, malicious PR, or GitHub token leak), every user running `browser-use init` would execute attacker-controlled code. signals.title: CI workflow pins a reusable action to a mutable branch tag instead of a commit SHA
signals.excerpt: Found by the source-only security audit of `nix-lib` at [`4fe2d00`](https://github.com/hoprnet/nix-lib/commit/4fe2d00f5baa76ddbb5adbdbb5244b750a42274b) (default branch HEAD). **Severity: Medium** ### Summary The only CI workflow consumes a reusable action from a sibling HOPR repository via a mutable moving ref: `uses: hoprnet/hopr-workflows/actions/nix-action@nix-action-v1` (`.github/workflows/nix-checks.yaml:20`), while passing `cachix_auth_token: ` in its `with:` block (`:23-24`). Any future compromise of `hoprnet/hopr-workflows` (direct push, tag re-point, or maintainer account takeover) silently changes what executes with access to that secret. The repository's Dependabot config (`.github/dependabot.yml`) only covers the `nix-flake-inputs` group, so GitHub Actions refs are not tracked for updates either — the tag is neither SHA-pinned nor auto-bumped. ### Fix Replace the ref with the full commit SHA the tag currently points to (`uses: hoprnet/hopr-workflows/actions/nix-action@ `, comment the version beside it), and add a `github-actions` entry to `.github/dependabot.yml` so updates arrive as reviewable PRs.

signals.title: Should I pin my Python dependencies versions?
signals.excerpt: I am about to release a Python library I've been working on the past few weeks. I've read a lot about Python dependencies but something is not quite clear yet: Some people pretend you should never pin your dependencies versions as it would prevent the users of your library from upgrading those dependencies. I somehow went for an hybrid solution, where I assumed my dependencies used semantic versioning and pinned only the major version number (say somelib >= 2.3.0, < 3 ) except when the major version number is 0 (semantic versioning dictates that such versions are to be considered volatile and may break the API even if only the patch number is bumped).
