briefs.researchQuestion: AI tools make it nearly free to open pull requests, issues and security reports. How much extra work does that create for open-source maintainers, and what could reduce it without shutting out genuine newcomers?
briefs.whyItMatters: Widely used open-source software depends on small groups of maintainers whose review time is scarce. Several well-known projects have responded by restricting or closing outside contributions entirely, which also cuts off the path by which new contributors become future maintainers.
subQuestions: How widespread is the burden, and what form does it take (pull requests, issues, security reports)?
Do projects object to the use of AI itself, or to unreviewed work that contributors don't understand?
Can a cheap, automatic signal separate low-effort submissions from genuine ones?
Can cheap signals, available before anyone reads a PR, make triage cheaper without excluding genuine newcomers?
Which interventions reduce the burden without excluding newcomers?

findings.statement: The burden is reported across many independent projects. tldraw, Rust, Astropy, LLVM, the Linux kernel, Ghostty, scikit-learn and Zulip all describe AI-generated contributions as consuming scarce review time. tldraw went as far as automatically closing all external pull requests.
findings.strength: Strong as a reported problem: the policies and statements of eight independent projects agree. They are maintainers' accounts, not measurements of volume or hours.

findings.statement: Projects mostly don't object to AI itself. They object to unreviewed work that the contributor doesn't understand. A study of 281 project AI policies found 83.3% permit AI in code contributions, and 67.3% require a high level of human involvement.
findings.strength: Strong: a systematic study of 281 policies, consistent with the individual policies of Ghostty, Zulip and curl.

findings.statement: Whether an author replies to maintainers is only a weak signal of a low-effort pull request. Within LLVM, authors of PRs later closed under the AI policy replied 80.9% of the time, against 90.2% for accepted newcomers.
findings.strength: Moderate. Measured by VENTURE's own experiment (180 PRs with comments), but the pre-registered verdict was inconclusive, and the within-LLVM comparison was exploratory.

findings.statement: Over a quarter of the policy-closed pull requests sampled (33 of 120) were closed without any human comment. Maintainers often dismiss them silently, which suggests much of the cost is in triage rather than in-depth review.
findings.strength: Weak to moderate. The count is measured, but the interpretation hasn't been tested.

findings.statement: Where repositories adopt AI coding agents, newcomers' share of participation drops by about 3.7 percentage points, while the absolute number of human contributors doesn't change significantly.
findings.strength: Moderate. One large study (11,097 repositories), and it measures agent adoption by the repository itself, which only indirectly concerns inbound contributions.

findings.statement: Fabricated, AI-generated security reports are a separate and severe drain: curl stopped offering a bug bounty, saying it rewarded made-up problems.
findings.strength: Weak. Only curl's own documents could be retrieved, so this is one independent origin.

findings.statement: Triage cost is now closing newcomer on-ramps. Astropy maintainers proposed retiring their 'good first issue' labels because triaging mostly unacceptable, usually AI-generated PRs costs more than the labels gain. Other projects are proposing one-click autoclose labels (scikit-learn) and instant closure of PRs that strip AI-disclosure checkboxes (nixpkgs).
findings.strength: Moderate. Three independent projects' own issue trackers. Proposals, not measured savings.

findings.statement: Blunt AI rules carry a fairness cost: a Kubernetes contributor argues they exclude people with disabilities who rely on AI as assistive technology. This favours behaviour-based triage that keeps humans in the decision over rules keyed on AI use.
findings.strength: Weak. One argued case, but it points to a real design constraint.

findings.statement: Cheap account-level signals are poor triage tools. Authors of policy-violating PRs had typically opened more PRs elsewhere in the prior month (median 6 vs 1), but the groups overlap so much that the signal's AUC is only 0.64. Account age is close to useless (0.54). Catching half of the problem PRs this way would also flag about 30% of genuine newcomers.
findings.strength: Moderate. A pre-registered test on 237 labelled PRs. The control group is LLVM-only, and per-PR data wasn't persisted.

findings.statement: What a PR says is a slightly better clue than who sent it. Policy-violating PRs had much longer descriptions (median 166 vs 87 words; AUC 0.67), matching maintainers' complaints about verbose AI output. Whether the PR references an issue made no difference.
findings.strength: Moderate. A pre-registered test on 240 labelled PRs. Still below the bar for a usable triage signal.

findings.statement: Combining the two best cheap signals doesn't fix the problem. An unfitted combination of description length and recent cross-repo PR count reached AUC 0.69, just below the pre-registered 0.70 line, and would flag about a quarter of genuine newcomers.
findings.strength: Moderate. The third pre-registered test on the same 240 labelled PRs. LLVM-only control group.

uncertainties: No direct measurement of how many AI-generated contributions projects receive, or how much time they cost, has been found.
Selection bias: projects that wrote AI policies are the ones most affected. Projects that see no problem are under-represented.
Several empirical studies use a dataset of agent-authored PRs that differs from unsolicited contributions to popular projects.
News coverage and blogs couldn't be read from the research environment, so secondary reporting (e.g. a reported Linux Foundation estimate) remains unverified.

conclusion.belief: The burden is real and widespread, and much of it is triage: deciding which PRs deserve attention at all. Projects largely accept AI help and object to unreviewed, low-understanding work, so detecting AI is the wrong lever, and blunt AI rules carry a fairness cost. VENTURE tested whether cheap, automatic signals could take over part of that triage: author follow-up, recent PR volume elsewhere, account age, issue references, description length, and a combination. None separates low-effort from genuine contributions well enough without flagging many genuine newcomers. The main contribution of this area is that negative result: tools built on such signals are unlikely to triage reliably. Judging contributions still needs a human, or a much deeper signal than these.
conclusion.confidenceReason: Medium: four pre-registered tests on real PRs agree that cheap signals are weak (best AUC 0.67–0.69). It's not high because the control group is LLVM-only, and deeper signals (e.g. reading the code change itself) weren't tested.
unknowns: Whether deeper, content-aware analysis of the code change would discriminate better
How much maintainer time triage actually takes
conclusion.continueReason: Paused, as the pre-registered rule required. Reopen if maintainer triage time is measured, if GitHub ships contribution-management features worth evaluating, or if new evidence links to the parked or rejected ideas.

nextSteps.text: None scheduled: the solution search is paused. The reconsideration queue will surface parked and rejected ideas if new evidence arrives.
Optional: validate the negative result on a non-LLVM control group before publishing it more widely.

briefs.author: research director (Claude Code session)

briefs.researchQuestion: Libraries regularly ship 'minor' or 'patch' updates that break the code of everyone using them, even though those updates are installed automatically on the promise of being safe. Could a small open-source tool catch these breaks before a release is published?
briefs.whyItMatters: Every JavaScript project depends on dozens to hundreds of packages and trusts version numbers to signal risk. When a minor release breaks that trust, users lose time pinning versions and debugging, and maintainers lose credibility. Rust has a widely adopted tool for this; JavaScript has no established equivalent.
subQuestions: How often do popular npm packages ship breaking changes in minor or patch releases?
What kinds of breaks are they: type changes, behaviour changes, or metadata changes?
What do existing and emerging tools catch, and what do they miss?
Is there a small, buildable tool that catches a meaningful share with little noise?

findings.statement: Breaking minor and patch releases cost users real time. Reports describe whole codebases breaking after a React minor update, release pipelines broken for a weekend, and maintainers forced to pin versions. Microsoft built API Extractor partly because users 'keep reporting that their code won't compile after a supposedly minor update'.
findings.strength: Moderate. Several independent reports plus Microsoft's own stated motivation. Individual cases, not a measured rate.

findings.statement: The tool model works elsewhere: Rust's cargo-semver-checks (about 1,700 stars, with a GitHub Action) checks releases for semver violations, though it documents breaks it can't catch.
findings.strength: Strong as evidence that a tool exists and is adopted in Rust. It doesn't show JS maintainers would adopt one.

findings.statement: The TypeScript type-surface checker niche is filling up: Clerk's break-check (company-backed), ts-semver-checks and semver-check all appeared in 2026, alongside Microsoft's API Extractor.
findings.strength: Strong for existence. All are very new, with little adoption yet.

findings.statement: Type checkers miss many real breaks. None of the four complaints examined was a type change: they were behaviour changes (React, floating-ui, node-abort-controller) and a metadata change (polished raised its required Node version in a minor release).
findings.strength: Weak to moderate. A small sample, but it points to a clear gap: the install and import contract in package metadata.

findings.statement: Metadata-level contract breaks are common: by the linter's rules, 20% of 400 popular npm packages shipped at least one in a minor or patch release over two years. But as specified the rules are too noisy: only 8 of 20 audited flags were genuine breaks. Most of the rest were debatable engine-range changes dropping end-of-life Node versions.
findings.strength: Moderate. A pre-registered measurement plus a hand audit of 20 flags against criteria fixed beforehand (one reviewer).

findings.statement: The structural rules are the useful core. Removed export paths, entry fields and CLI commands, and tightened peers, were genuine in 7 of 9 audited cases, but they fire for only about 10% of popular packages over two years. Many flags come from a few fast-moving projects (@tanstack, better-auth, @typescript-eslint).
findings.strength: Weak to moderate. Exploratory, post hoc, small n.

uncertainties: How often metadata-level breaks actually happen in popular packages (being measured).
Whether maintainers consider deliberate engine bumps in minor releases acceptable.
The four complaints were chosen by GitHub search ranking, not sampled randomly.

conclusion.belief: Accidental breaking releases are real, and a cheap metadata check can catch a share of them that type checkers miss: removed export paths, entry points and CLI commands, and tightened peers. But it's a modest benefit (about 1 in 10 popular packages over two years). As first specified, engine-range rules make it too noisy. The practical value is a small, precise rule set, best contributed as a 'compare with last release' mode to an existing packaging linter such as publint. That would be useful open-source work, but not a standalone product.
conclusion.confidenceReason: A pre-registered measurement over 12,240 release pairs plus an audited sample. Not high: the audit had one reviewer and 20 flags, and the narrowed rule set's precision comes from only 9 audited cases.
unknowns: The narrowed rule set's precision on a fresh sample
Whether publint's maintainers would want this feature
How often flagged breaks actually hurt users (issues filed after release)
conclusion.continueReason: One cheap step remains: validate the narrowed rule set on a fresh, independently drawn audit sample before proposing it upstream.

nextSteps.text: Validate the structural-only rule set on a fresh random sample of 20 flags not in the first audit (pre-registered: ≥ 70% genuine).
If it holds, prototype a 'compare with last release' check, and ask the owner whether VENTURE may propose it to the publint maintainers. That means contacting people, so it needs authorization.

briefs.researchQuestion: When attackers take over a maintainer's account or publishing credentials, they can push malware to everyone who installs the next release. What can volunteer maintainers without a security team realistically do to catch this?
briefs.whyItMatters: In 2026, compromised releases of very widely used packages (axios on npm, litellm on PyPI, asyncapi and TanStack packages) installed remote-access trojans or stole credentials. The maintainers were victims, not insiders. Most open-source maintainers have no security staff to notice when a release they didn't make appears.
subQuestions: How do these compromises happen, and how long do malicious releases stay live?
What already protects consumers (release delays, trusted publishing), and what gaps remain?
Do hijacked releases look structurally different from a maintainer's normal releases, so that a simple alarm could catch them?

findings.statement: Compromised maintainer accounts and tokens are a recurring route to malware in popular packages. At least four 2026 incidents were found, including axios (a remote-access trojan via an injected dependency) and litellm (a credential stealer).
findings.strength: Moderate. Four independent incident reports, taken from the projects' own issue trackers.

findings.statement: Malicious releases are typically live for hours: about 3 hours for axios. Delaying installs of brand-new versions is an effective defence that users actively ask for, and the platforms are already shipping it (pnpm, Dependabot cooldown).
findings.strength: Moderate. Feature requests with hundreds of reactions, and a study finding 83 of 92 cooldown adoptions were security-motivated.

findings.statement: Most hijacks of legitimate npm packages add an install-time hook (a script that runs on install), something legitimate releases almost never do. Across 15 independent attack campaigns (2024–2026) whose mechanism could be determined, 12 (80%) added such a hook, versus 1.7% of legitimate releases of the same packages.
findings.strength: Moderate. A pre-registered replication at campaign level supports an earlier package-level result. But it rests on the minimum sample of 15 campaigns, and 7 more campaigns had no described mechanism (the share could be anywhere from 55% to 86%).

findings.statement: About one in five characterisable campaigns would slip past such an alarm: asyncapi, node-ipc and netspeedutil injected code into existing files without adding hooks or dependencies.
findings.strength: Moderate. 3 of 15 classifiable campaigns, consistent with the earlier asyncapi counter-example.

findings.statement: Teams that adopt release delays overwhelmingly use one simple default (most often seven days). Fine-grained settings are used by fewer than 10%.
findings.strength: Moderate. One study of early adopters.

findings.statement: The platforms have started to close the stolen-token route themselves. Since May 2026, npm lets maintainers require a human 2FA approval for every release (staged publishing) and forbid publishing with tokens. Since 2024, PyPI emails maintainers when a token uploads to a project that uses trusted publishing.
findings.strength: Strong for existence: the registries' own documentation and code. Adoption is unknown and opt-in.

findings.statement: npm's new protections are barely adopted. Half of 400 popular npm packages (50.2%) published their latest release with neither trusted publishing nor staged human approval, and only 7.8% use staged approval. Even 13 of 22 packages that were actually hijacked still publish this way.
findings.strength: Moderate. A pre-registered measurement on public registry data. 'Neither' is an upper bound on exposure, because interactive 2FA publishes look the same in the metadata.

uncertainties: 'Neither' publishing practice is an upper bound on token exposure: interactive 2FA publishes can't be told apart in registry metadata.
Whether security vendors offer maintainer-side release alerts. Their public tooling is consumer-side, and their product sites couldn't be read.
Campaign grouping is heuristic, and 7 of 22 campaigns had no described mechanism.
The incident sample favours large, well-publicised attacks.

conclusion.belief: Account and token compromise of popular packages is a severe and recurring problem. Three pre-registered experiments support the case for a maintainer-side alarm: most independent hijack campaigns add an install-time hook that legitimate releases rarely add, and about half of popular npm packages still publish without npm's new protections, so the alarm would have a large audience. What isn't known yet is whether maintainers want such alerts and would act on them, how noisy the alerts would be in practice, and whether vendors already offer this. The alarm also can't catch attacks that only modify existing files.
conclusion.confidenceReason: The technical premise and the audience are each supported by pre-registered experiments on public data. Demand, alert volume and the competitive landscape are untested. Those need either a field test or contact with maintainers.
unknowns: How often the alarm would fire on ordinary releases (alert fatigue)
Whether maintainers want such alerts and act on them
Whether vendors already offer maintainer-side alerts
How to catch attacks that only modify existing files
conclusion.continueReason: A no-cost prospective field test can measure alert volume next. Testing maintainer demand needs the owner's authorization.

nextSteps.text: A 28-day prospective field test is running: it measures how often the alarm would fire on real releases of 400 popular npm packages. Results are expected around 2026-12-02.
If alert volume is manageable, ask the owner to authorize a small test of maintainer interest. This involves contacting people.
Verify vendor offerings once their sites are reachable from the research environment.
